hints: A path through every cell alternates checkerboard colors, so the endpoint colors are constrained.
Thin rectangles have extra impossible cases even when their endpoint colors fit.
Use a rectangle Hamilton-path feasibility test, then recursively cut the rectangle or splice in a two-column strip.
analogy: A path can be assembled like a tour through two rooms: cross their common wall exactly once, or replace one boundary edge by a detour through a strip.
example: In a 2x2 grid, the top-left and bottom-right corners have the same color, so they cannot be the endpoints of a four-cell path. Top-left to bottom-left works with RDL.
algorithm: Use zero-based coordinates, with x as the column and y as the row. Rotate so height h<=width w, and order the endpoints so x1<=x2. A single-cell rectangle is feasible when its endpoints coincide; larger rectangles cannot have coincident endpoints. A one-row grid is feasible only when the endpoints are its two ends. For height 2, endpoints in the same column are feasible only at an outermost column; otherwise their checkerboard colors must differ. For odd area, both endpoints must have even x+y. For even area with height at least 4, colors must differ. For height 3 and even area, colors must differ; additionally reject when the left endpoint has odd x+y and either x1<x2-1, or x1<x2 and y1=1. For a feasible rectangle, normalize by reflection, handle one-row and small at-most-4x5 rectangles using precomputed exhaustive paths, and handle adjacent endpoints on a two-row board by a direct perimeter snake. Otherwise try removing a two-column strip away from both endpoints when the remainder is feasible: recursively solve the remainder, replace a vertical boundary edge by a snake through the strip, and reconnect it. If no strip applies, try horizontal or vertical cuts between endpoints and a crossing pair of adjacent cells for which both subrectangles pass the same feasibility test; recursively concatenate their paths and the crossing step. Undo the rotations/reflections in the output.
correctness: The checkerboard and thin-board tests are the rectangular grid Hamilton-path characterization. The strip operation replaces one path edge by a detour covering exactly the removed cells. Each cut joins two disjoint full-coverage paths by one edge, so the result visits every cell exactly once. The rectangular-grid construction theorem guarantees an applicable strip or feasible cut for the remaining non-base cases.
complexity: For an n by m rectangle, a direct implementation that scans candidate cuts and materializes recursive paths takes O((nm)^2) time and space in a conservative bound, including output; the base cases are fixed-size.
